rule: Typed receivers (decision A ...): a receiver whose type is given by a declaration ... gives `T#m` ... `self.m()` / `this.m()` / a bare call to a member of the enclosing type → `Type#m`. ... Call through a parameter ... holding a function ... → callee is the variable's name, `call_type` callback, confidence unknown. ... Decisions (2026-10-29): each picks what the code does at runtime
source: KNOWN_GAP: bare calls on implicit lambda receivers (apply {}, buildMap {}) are attributed to the outer receiver
notes: call_type convention (SPEC names the six call_types but does not define direct vs method): a call with no written receiver is direct; a call with a written receiver (obj., this., super., a type or object name) is method; a class-name call `T(..)` that resolves to a constructor, and `: this(..)` / `: super(..)` / a supertype-list call, are constructor. Kotlin has no `new`; a `val x = T(..)` constructor call is treated as decision A's `= new T(...)`. The lambda passed to `cfg.edit { .. }` has declared receiver type `Config.() -> Unit`. Its innermost implicit receiver is a Config, so at runtime the bare `setName("svc")` (line 20) runs Config#setName, not App#setName, though App also defines setName. That is the gap: the tool names the outer receiver. The lambda folds into App#build, so the caller is App#build. Line 22 is outside the lambda: App#setName. `block()` invokes a function-typed parameter: `block`, callback, unknown. A scanned higher-order member stands in for apply/buildMap here because SPEC does not decide IDs for Kotlin standard-library functions (see case 16).
